{{nihongo|'''Ogura Shrine'''|小椋神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Ōmi Province]].

It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}}, and under the former {{ill|Q712534|lt=shrine ranking system}} it was a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural Shrine}}.

In addition to Ogura Shrine, four other shrines are enshrined here: Ōmiya Shrine, Wakamiya Shrine, Imamiya Shrine, and Shingū Shrine.

=== History ===
According to shrine tradition, during the transfer of the capital to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōmi-kyō}} in Emperor {{ill|Emperor Tenji|Q314802|qid=Q314802}} 6 ({{ill|667|Q30702|qid=Q30702}}), an ascetic called Kadaifu (also written Gadaifu/Kadaifu) Sennin, who accompanied the move, invited a {{ill|Bunrei|Q195793|qid=Q195793}} from {{ill|Niukawakami Shrine (Q246370)|Q246370|qid=Q246370}} in {{ill|Yamato Province|Q907495|qid=Q907495}} to Ogi, marking the foundation. Later, in {{ill|Jōgan|Q1075635|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} 1 ({{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}}), it is said to have been moved to the present site by {{ill|Minamoto no Tōru|Q1284268|qid=Q1284268}}. The present site is also said to have been where Ōmiya Shrine was founded a year earlier, in {{ill|Ten'an|Q1075611|qid=Q1075611|lt=Ten'an}} 2 ({{ill|858|Q30371|qid=Q30371}}), by Prince {{ill|Koretaka-shinnō|Q11492950|qid=Q11492950}}, son of {{ill|Emperor Montoku|Q357225|qid=Q357225}}. At the former site, Takitsubo Shrine, now the {{ill|Okumiya|Q11445659|qid=Q11445659}}, is enshrined ({{Coord|35|06|21.9|N|135|51|13.1|E|scale:25000}}). Later, in {{ill|Engi (era)|Q1374325|qid=Q1374325}} 2 ({{ill|902|Q23587|qid=Q23587}}), Wakamiya Shrine was enshrined.

In Engi 8 ({{ill|908|Q30463|qid=Q30463}}), it was listed as an {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Engishiki shikinaisha}}.

In {{ill|Jōgen (Heian period)|Q1324833|qid=Q1324833|lt=Jōgen}} 2 ({{ill|977|Q23795|qid=Q23795}}), {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|Q2531241|qid=Q2531241}} moved to this area and stayed for ten years.

In {{ill|Kenkyū|Q1193933|qid=Q1193933}} 1 ({{ill|1190|Q19736|qid=Q19736}}), Imamiya Shrine and Shingū Shrine were enshrined in the precincts. In the medieval period, it was also called '''Gosha Daigongen''' ('''Daimyōjin''') and drew devotion.

In {{ill|1876|Q7766|qid=Q7766}} (Meiji 9), it was ranked as a {{ill|Son-sha|ja|村社|qid=Q134917284}}. In {{ill|1908|Q2056|qid=Q2056}} (Meiji 41), it was designated a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shinsen-heihaku-ryō kyōshinsha}}. The shrine name had at some point become '''Tadosho Shrine''', but in {{ill|1945|Q5240|qid=Q5240}} ({{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} 20) it was restored to the current name and promoted to prefectural shrine<ref>{{Cite web|和書|url=http://ogurajinja.org/yuisyo.html |title=Ogura Shrine History |accessdate=2012-12-23}}</ref>.

=== Festivals ===
* Annual festival (May 3)
:: Called the '''Ogi Festival'''. Because it often rains and the route after the mikoshi procession becomes like a muddy field, it is also called the '''Muddy Field Festival'''. It includes an old-style rite commemorating {{ill|Minamoto no Mitsunaka|Q2531241|qid=Q2531241}}, second generation of the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|Q2164991|qid=Q2164991}} who moved to Ogi in the late {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, as well as {{ill|Yabusame|Q1886157|qid=Q1886157}} and processions of mikoshi from five shrines.
